Both files must print `synced=True` or `already in sync`. Then `git hash-object AGENTS.md` equals `git hash-object CLAUDE.md`.

STEP 2 - Lockfile policy statement. The operator created an enterprise Actions policy named "Actions Lockfile" (rule: Require lockfile; every organization, repository and workflow; enforcement: Evaluate). Evaluate records, under Policy insights, the runs that Active mode would block, and blocks none. In the CHANGELOG Unreleased section, find the clause stating that the `Require lockfile` policy stays off (English: "stays off", "remains off", "continues disabled"; Portuguese: "permanece desligada", "continua desativada", "segue desligada") and replace ONLY that clause, grammatical in its own language:
  - English: "The `Require lockfile` policy runs in **Evaluate** mode at the enterprise."
  - Portuguese: "A política `Require lockfile` roda em modo **Evaluate** no enterprise."
Do the same in any README, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY or THIRDPARTY sentence carrying that statement. If nothing carries it, change nothing and say so. Dated historical CHANGELOG entries stay.

STEP 3 - Verification job. Create `.github/workflows/verify-lockfile.yml` with exactly this content:

name: verify-lockfile

on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: github/gh-actions-lock@5fa07d19c267d19e29f4341f10fdf7f516375038 # verify/v0.5.1

This is the official example of the `github/gh-actions-lock` repository (README and verify/README.md). Exactly two adaptations are allowed, and only when the repository already uses a different convention in its other workflows:
  (a) `runs-on`: the runner label this repository's other Linux jobs use; otherwise keep `ubuntu-latest`.
  (b) permissions: `permissions: {}` at the top level and `permissions: contents: read` on the job; the effective grant must stay `contents: read`.
Nothing else changes: no path filter, no `paths-ignore`, no push trigger, no extra inputs, no `continue-on-error`. Write `verify/v0.5.1` as the version (the tag `verify/v*` is the one the documentation says to pin). Match the file's indentation style of the repository's other workflows only if it differs (spaces); the content above is already the YAML the documentation shows.
If `.github/workflows/verify-lockfile.yml` already exists on this branch, verify it equals this content and skip the creation.

It must add the new workflow and its two dependencies to `.github/workflows/actions.lock`. Follow the file's row or prose convention; keep tracked copies byte-identical.
  b. Workflow lists. Where a README, CONTRIBUTING, SECURITY or docs section enumerates this repository's workflows or its pull-request checks, add the new workflow as a check that runs on every pull request and reports without blocking. Where nothing enumerates workflows, add nothing.
  c. CHANGELOG. Add ONE Unreleased entry, in this repository's language, stating: the repository now runs the official `verify-lockfile` workflow on every pull request through `github/gh-actions-lock`, which fails when `actions.lock` is out of sync with the workflows or a locked pin no longer verifies upstream; it reports and does not block, because it is not a required check (LCV-738).

Then every local gate this repository defines that reads the files this branch changed: the exact commands CI runs (from .github/workflows/ci.yml, package.json or the build files), including any test that reads the workflows or the documentation. iOS: never run Xcode or simulators; declare them as validation gaps. When a gate exits non-zero, classify it: caused by this branch (fix it), pre-existing at the base (prove by stash and re-run; out of scope), or environmental (prove which; validation gap). Never report a gate as passed when it did not run or did not pass.

Write the message to temp/commit-msg.txt (Conventional Commits, US English, the trailer `Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>` as the last line). Suggested title: `ci(lockfile): verify actions.lock on every pull request and sync the workspace instructions`. The body states what you did in steps 1 to 5. `git add` each changed file by name (never temp/). Commit with `git commit -S -F temp/commit-msg.txt`. Verify with `git log -1 --format=%B` that the `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer exists and with `git for-each-ref "refs/entire/checkpoints/**"` that its ref exists locally. Never pass --no-verify. Never run `entire session attach`.

STEP 8 - STOP. Do not push, do not open a pull request, do not create temp/pr-body.md.

Keep them: read `git status --porcelain` and `git diff`, finish what is incomplete, correct what is wrong, and include all of it in your commit. If any was rewritten to a tag, restore that workflow file with `git checkout origin/main -- <file>` and run `gh actions-lock --no-narrow` again. Never a plain `gh actions-lock`.

Every file that lists the GitHub Actions this repository runs (THIRDPARTY.md and each tracked copy, `git ls-files "*THIRDPARTY*"`; any README, CONTRIBUTING or SECURITY section that names Action versions) agrees with the live `uses:` pins and with the `dependencies:` section of actions.lock:

Complete it if it is missing or unfinished. The entry STEP 5c asks for is a separate, additional entry.

This inventory covers every external GitHub Action invoked by the repository
workflows, the CI-only npm and browser validation tooling, and the externally
hosted components used by the profile or the Pages site. The repository's
package manifest contains only development tooling for browser-level
provenance tests. No npm package, browser binary, or FFmpeg binary is copied

GitHub checks the locked commit for an onboarded workflow and a lockfile satisfies the SHA-pinning policy by itself, so the in-file SHA is the fleet's reviewed record, not the enforcement point; keep it so the reviewed pin survives deletion of the lockfile and stays readable in review ([Governing execution of GitHub Actions workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/control-workflow-execution#require-lockfile)). Generate and refresh with **`gh actions-lock --no-narrow`**; a plain run rewrites the pins to version tags and is forbidden here. The **Require lockfile** policy exists at the enterprise in **Evaluate** mode: under Policy insights it records the workflow runs that **Active** mode would block; move it to **Active** only after every targeted repository passes `gh actions-lock --verify` (same page). The extension locks external actions and the actions a `$/` path uses. A local path action (`uses: ./…`) runs whatever is checked out in the runner's workspace, so the extension can neither pin it nor see what it uses. When such an action uses other actions, the extension stops with a `local-action` error before writing the lockfile, so take one of the two documented decisions — `--migrate-local-actions`, which rewrites the reference to the inherently pinned `uses: $/…` form, or an explicit `--ignore-local-actions` — and record which one in the pull request ([Locking action dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/lock-workflow-dependencies)). ## Operational baseline

This repository follows the LCV Ideas & Software single-operator security baseline:

- GitHub secret scanning and push protection;
- Dependabot alerts and security updates;
- GitHub code scanning default setup for CodeQL;
- external GitHub Actions pinned by full commit SHA with a version comment in every `uses:`. Beyond the
  committed npm lockfile, `.github/workflows/actions.lock` records each action's exact commit, the source
  repository identity and the transitive dependencies no workflow file references. It is generated with
  `gh actions-lock --no-narrow`, never hand-edited, and refreshed by Dependabot in the same pull request
  ([workflow dependency lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles));
- workflow-level `permissions: {}` with the least `GITHUB_TOKEN` grant required by each job;
- direct, SHA-pinned official Dependency Review, Zizmor, and OpenSSF Scorecard Actions. CodeQL default setup remains the native merge-protection signal; Zizmor and Scorecard publish SARIF for security visibility without repository-owned gates, baselines, wrappers, or workflow-contract validators. The native Actions lockfile above is GitHub's own mechanism, not a repository-owned gate;
- the official Zizmor Action does not yet expose `--strict-collection` ([upstream #141](https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-action/issues/141)), so collection syntax or schema errors can remain warnings. This accepted upstream limitation is tracked without adding a repository-owned executor or gate;
- external credentials assigned by purpose to protected environments restricted to `main`, with one
  documented exception: the Dependabot auto-merge workflow reads a fine-grained personal
  access token (Contents, Pull requests and Workflows, read and write) from the Dependabot secret
  `DEPENDABOT_AUTOMERGE_TOKEN`, because a workflow triggered by a Dependabot pull request can read
  Dependabot secrets only. GitHub does not inject these values automatically: an authorized job
  receives a secret only when its workflow explicitly references it. The auto-merge workflow runs
  only on Dependabot's own pull requests from this repository, grants no `GITHUB_TOKEN`
  permission, binds the arming request to the exact event head, fails visibly when the run carries no
  Dependabot secret (the secret is not configured, or the event was initiated by a person), and
  runs no Action, checkout, cache, artifact, or pull-request-controlled command. Fork and
  non-Dependabot pull requests never run it. The `Claude Code` workflow holds no credential: it
  authenticates by workload identity federation, as described under Automation policy;
- pull requests, squash-only merges, signed commits, linear history, resolved conversations, and required checks enforced by the repository's own rulesets, which mirror the organization's Enterprise rulesets because a personal repository inherits none of them;
- no long-lived secrets in source control.

### Personal-account product boundaries

GitHub secret scanning and push protection are enabled for this public repository. GitHub currently limits validity checks and generic/non-provider pattern scanning to eligible organization-owned repositories with GitHub Secret Protection; the corresponding settings therefore remain `PRODUCT_UNAVAILABLE` for this user-owned repository. An API response that accepts an update without changing the readback is not treated as successful enablement.

### Contribution-snake provenance boundary

The profile's contribution snake is generated by the repository-owned, zero-dependency `scripts/generate-contribution-snake.mjs`. Pull requests exercise it only against local fixtures, and the browser provenance tests call GitHub's public Markdown renderer without authentication; their test job grants only `contents: read`, checkout does not persist credentials, and no token is passed to either test process. Trusted `main`, scheduled, and manual Pages runs pass the ephemeral `GITHUB_TOKEN` separately to the provenance renderer and to the generator that queries GitHub's GraphQL contribution calendar. The token has read-only repository permissions, generated SVGs are treated as build artifacts, and the separate deploy job contains only GitHub-owned actions, runs only for `main`, and is the sole holder of `pages: write` and `id-token: write`.

## Automation policy

Dependabot checks every supported ecosystem every day, including weekends, at 05:00 in Brasília (`Etc/GMT+3`) using its native cron schedule. It groups minor and patch version updates per ecosystem, groups security updates separately without restricting their SemVer level, automatically rebases its pull requests, and relies on GitHub's post-merge branch deletion. Every dependency is excluded from the cooldown (`*` inside each `package-ecosystem` block), so ordinary version updates are proposed immediately and a release can be adopted as soon as its provenance, security, and compatibility are validated; the cooldown stays configured as a deliberate switch — replacing the `*` with narrower dependency-name patterns re-enables the delay for exactly what those patterns match. Dependabot security updates are triggered when vulnerabilities are detected, independently of the version-update schedule. Required security and quality checks are never bypassed.

Dependabot pull requests are the only automatically admitted change. The repository-local workflow `.github/workflows/dependabot-auto-merge.yml` runs on Dependabot's own `pull_request` events with no `GITHUB_TOKEN` permission, no Action, and no checkout, and enables GitHub's native auto-merge (squash) on the pull request with a fine-grained personal access token stored as the Dependabot secret `DEPENDABOT_AUTOMERGE_TOKEN`. GitHub performs the merge only after every rule of the effective rulesets and every required check is satisfied; the workflow cannot bypass rules, merge directly, update branches, or process forks or any other author. The auto-merge path uses no GitHub App, merge queue, organization-wide controller, or scheduler.

The repository-local workflow `.github/workflows/claude.yml` (`Claude Code`) runs the official `anthropics/claude-code-action`, pinned by full commit SHA, on `issue_comment` and `pull_request_review_comment` (created), `issues` (opened, assigned) and `pull_request_review` (submitted) events whose comment, review, issue title or issue body contains `@claude`, and never on pull requests opened by Dependabot (`dependabot[bot]`), whatever the request. The action acts only for a human actor with write access to the repository and rejects bot actors. Its job token has `contents`, `pull-requests` and `issues` write, `id-token` write and `actions` read; the `id-token` grant serves two OIDC exchanges, one for a token of the official Claude GitHub App installed on the `lcv-leo` account and one for a short-lived Claude API token. Its checkout keeps the default persisted job token, which the action's branch setup uses before it installs its own credential. It authenticates to the Claude API by workload identity federation: the job's GitHub OIDC token is exchanged for a short-lived Claude API token under an Anthropic federation rule that accepts only this repository and acts as one service account in one workspace, so the workflow holds only identifiers, no credential. It commits through the GitHub API with commit signing (`use_commit_signing: true`), may run no shell command other than the read-only `gh pr diff` and `gh pr view`, and is not a required check.

Repository-local workflows may secure and publish only this repository's own profile surfaces; organization or enterprise settings do not implicitly govern this personal account.

2. **Lockfiles:** as Section 6.B requires. GitHub Actions dependency lockfiles exist and are generally available: `.github/workflows/actions.lock`, generated only by the `gh actions-lock` CLI extension and never edited by hand, refreshed automatically by Dependabot inside the same version-update pull request ([Workflow dependency lockfiles](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles), [Locking action dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/lock-workflow-dependencies)). **Fleet position (operator decision, 25/11/2026):** every repository adopts the Actions lockfile **and keeps its `uses:` references pinned to a full-length commit SHA with the version comment**. GitHub checks the locked commit for an onboarded workflow and a lockfile satisfies the SHA-pinning policy by itself, so the in-file SHA is the fleet's reviewed record, not the enforcement point; keep it so the reviewed pin survives deletion of the lockfile and stays readable in review ([Governing execution of GitHub Actions workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/administer/control-workflow-execution#require-lockfile)). Generate and refresh with **`gh actions-lock --no-narrow`**; a plain run rewrites the pins to version tags and is forbidden here. The **Require lockfile** policy exists at the enterprise in **Evaluate** mode: under Policy insights it records the workflow runs that **Active** mode would block; move it to **Active** only after every targeted repository passes `gh actions-lock --verify` (same page). The extension locks external actions and the actions a `$/` path uses. A local path action (`uses: ./…`) runs whatever is checked out in the runner's workspace, so the extension can neither pin it nor see what it uses. When such an action uses other actions, the extension stops with a `local-action` error before writing the lockfile, so take one of the two documented decisions — `--migrate-local-actions`, which rewrites the reference to the inherently pinned `uses: $/…` form, or an explicit `--ignore-local-actions` — and record which one in the pull request ([Locking action dependencies](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/lock-workflow-dependencies)). A `$/` path runs at the workflow's own commit and is pinned by that commit. A routine `--no-narrow` change touches `actions.lock` only, but upstream renames and transfers rewrite `uses:` names and `--migrate-local-actions` edits workflows, so read the full diff. Every lockfile change still sweeps all eight surfaces of this section. The lockfile does not cover reusable-workflow calls (`jobs.<job_id>.uses`): a cross-repository call stays pinned by full commit SHA, while a same-repository `$/` or `./` call carries no `@ref` and runs at the caller's own commit ([Workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax)).
